newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's communist leader sees explosive New Year.
newsitem.headline: Russia's communist leader sees explosive New Year.

text.p: Softly, softly the spirit of revolution is stalking Russia, promising an explosive 1997 -- or so thinks Gennady Zyuganov, the communist leader defeated by Boris Yeltsin in last year's presidential election.
"It feels now like August 1917. No one saw the revolution coming, but it came in three months. By March 1997, things could blow up," he told Reuters in an end-of-year interview.
And, surprisingly perhaps for a student of Marx, he sees the influence of the stars, as much as politics or economics, making the discontent of Russia's suffering millions boil over.
Toasting the New Year with his family at their spacious but plain Moscow apartment, the portly former maths teacher said he had no wish to foment revolt.

But the five-year civil war which followed the Bolshevik revolution in 1917 remains a vivid lesson for Zyuganov and he often refers to his childhood in the devastated plains of western Russia after World War Two.

"We must never return to that," he said, sipping sparkling wine beside a fir tree hung with hammer and sickle baubles and surrounded by icons that reflect the Orthodox Christian ideas of his married daughter Tatyana, who lives at home.
Zyuganov, 52, said Yeltsin and his followers would have to watch their step because, as in 1917, the army was in no mood to defend the country's rulers.
He echoed Yeltsin, who has declared 1997 the "Year of Reconciliation and Accord", by calling for compromise.

Yet Zyuganov, who urged a government of "national accord" during the election campaign, feared a force stronger than the Kremlin will stir unrest among millions of Russians for whom market reforms have brought poverty and chaos.
"It's well known there is an 11-year cycle of sun spot activity which influences society," he said, referring to some of the historical and scientific works he reads for relaxation.

"We've been in a very quiet phase. That's why things have been calm in Russia. But we're approaching a very disturbed period. By 1999, it will be very tough," Zyuganov forecast as he stroked the family's plump ginger tom-cat, Vasily.
By then, he may be preparing a new tilt at the presidency. Yeltsin's new four-year term ends in mid-2000.
Zyuganov, who has a photograph of the Kremlin's spires on his living room wall, refused to see 1996 as a year of defeat even though he lost the presidential election last July.

The year began with the communists taking a hold on the State Duma lower house after a parliamentary election in December 1995 and ended with them doing well in regional polls which could give them a grip on the upper house.
"People all around the country from all walks of life are uniting behind us. That's a great success," Zyuganov said.

Some politicians have suggested there is a new spirit of cooperation between the communists and the Kremlin. But Zyuganov has maintained his avowed animosity towards Yeltsin and even criticised the president's leisure-time activities.
"He plays tennis, which develops individualism," Zyuganov said. "I prefer collective games, like volleyball."
Yeltsin's energetic dancing during his election campaign, which helped win the youth vote but may have worsened his heart problems, also earned Zyuganov's scorn.
The communist leader prefers Russian folk dancing. But his wife Nadezhda chided: "His belly gets in the way."
